897.title: Whitefield in the fields
897.hook: a cross-eyed actor-preacher heard by crowds in the open air
897.howItsDone: Open-air preaching is still part of some evangelical and Methodist life, from street corners to summer camp meetings, and Whitefield is remembered by Anglicans, Methodists and evangelicals as a leading open-air preacher of the revival.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles Wesley's hymns. Your line was o for a thousand tongues. Did a line of an old hymn stay in your head? Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

A printer in Philadelphia is walking backward down a crowded street. Not for fun. He's measuring. Up the street, a young preacher stands on the courthouse steps, talking to a crowd packed into the open air, and the printer wants to know how far that one voice can carry before the noise of the city swallows it. No roof. No pews. No organ. Just weather, and a voice. The printer is Benjamin Franklin. The preacher is an Anglican clergyman with a squint in one eye and, as a boy, a love of the stage. Today: Whitefield in the fields.

George Whitefield belonged to the same circle at Oxford as John and Charles Wesley, the group their classmates mocked as the Methodists. When pulpits in England stopped inviting him, he walked out to a hillside where coal miners came up from the pits, and preached to whoever was standing there. Tradition says tears ran pale lines down the coal dust on their faces. Preaching outside was not something a respectable clergyman did. Whitefield did it anyway, and then talked John Wesley into trying it too. He crossed the ocean again and again, preaching up and down the American colonies in fields, town squares and market streets. What did he actually say? One line he came back to was Jesus's word in the Gospel of John: "Ye must be born again." Not a new church, not a new rule, but a new heart. People said he could make an audience weep just by the way he spoke a single word. Then there is Benjamin Franklin, no revivalist himself. In his autobiography, Franklin tells how he went to hear Whitefield and decided ahead of time not to give a penny to the collection. As the sermon went on he softened, first to copper coins, then to silver, and in the end, he writes, he emptied his pocket into the dish. The walk backward down the street comes from the same book. Whitefield's field preaching raised hard questions too. Some ministers said he stirred up feelings and left the churches to clean up after him. And later in life he owned enslaved people on a Georgia estate, and that belongs in his story. The open air took the sermon out of the building, to the pit head, the courthouse steps and the market.

Here's the practice: speak up clearly, once. Sit up, let your shoulders drop, and breathe low into your belly. On one out-breath, say a single sentence out loud, at full voice, as if to someone across a field. It can be your name, or a line you love. If you pray, you can make it a line from a psalm you know, and let it ring. Then sit in the quiet after it, and listen to how far the silence goes. The bell holds the time.
Whitefield in the fields. An Anglican preacher who left the pulpit for hillsides and town squares, and preached to whoever came, in the open air.
Your line: in the open air. Today, take one conversation you'd normally have indoors and have it outside, on a walk or a step. Notice what changes. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

898.title: Jonathan Edwards
898.hook: the Great Awakening in New England, and Edwards writing on religious affections
898.howItsDone: Edwards is read in Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist and evangelical churches and seminaries, and his Religious Affections is still used by pastors trying to tell real spiritual awakening from passing excitement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Whitefield in the fields. Your line was in the open air. Did you take a conversation outside, and did it change? Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

Honey on the tongue. You can read that honey is sweet. You can repeat it, believe it, pass a test on it. Or you can taste it. Same fact, two completely different kinds of knowing. A pastor in a small New England town used that picture, the taste of honey, to describe faith. Then his own church was stirred up. People were weeping, staying up late to pray, crowding his study with questions. Some neighbors called it a work of God. Others called it hysteria. He decided the honest thing was to sit down and think it through. Today: Jonathan Edwards.

Jonathan Edwards was a Congregationalist minister in Northampton, Massachusetts, during the season of revival people later called the Great Awakening, the same stirring that Whitefield preached into. Edwards is often remembered for one frightening sermon about sinners in the hands of an angry God. But much of his life went into a harder question: when a revival sweeps through a town, how do you tell what is real? He answered in a long book, A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections. Its claim is short: "True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections." By affections he did not mean passing moods. He meant the deep leanings of the heart, what a person loves, hates, hopes for and delights in. Faith, for Edwards, was not only an idea held in the head. In a sermon on a divine and supernatural light, he drew the difference that gives us our line. There is believing, as a matter of opinion, that God is holy and gracious, and there is having a sense of the heart, tasting it, the way a person who has eaten honey knows its sweetness in a way a reader never will. But here is the careful part. Edwards also warned that strong feelings prove nothing on their own. Tears, shaking, loud joy: none of them, he argued, settle whether something is from God. The chief sign, he wrote, is a changed life, the fruit of the heart showing up in ordinary practice, day after day. So he defended the feelings against the scoffers, and tested them against the enthusiasts. A sense of the heart, yes. Then watch what it does on Monday.
screen: `HOW DO YOU TELL WHAT IS REAL?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your heart's affections. Sit, and breathe slowly. Ask quietly: what am I leaning toward right now? What am I leaning away from? Don't fix anything. Just name it, the way you'd name a taste: wanting, dreading, delighting, longing. If you pray, you can hold what you find before God without dressing it up. If you don't, simply notice the leaning. The bell holds the time.
Jonathan Edwards. A New England pastor in the Great Awakening who wrote that true religion lives in holy affections, and that a changed life is the best test of them.
Your line: a sense of the heart. Today, when something moves you, a song, a kindness, a sunset, ask the second question too: what will this change by tonight? Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

the deep leanings of the heart

899.title: Joy to the world
899.hook: Isaac Watts wrote it as a psalm (Psalm 98), not originally for Christmas
899.howItsDone: Joy to the World is sung in Protestant and Catholic churches, usually at Christmas, though some churches also sing it in Advent or at other seasons as a hymn of Christ's rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonathan Edwards. Your line was a sense of the heart. When something moved you, did you ask what it changed? Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

A carol plays in a grocery store in December, between the canned cranberries and the wrapping paper. Joy to the world, the Lord is come. It gets filed under Christmas. Now listen again to the words. There's no manger in it. No shepherds, no star, no wise men, no baby at all. There's earth, heaven, fields and floods, rocks, hills and plains, and a king who rules the world. It reads less like a nativity scene and more like a coronation. That's because it began as something else. Today: Joy to the world.

Isaac Watts was an English minister among the Dissenters, the Protestants outside the Church of England. In his day, some of those churches sang only the Psalms, in versions kept close to the Bible's wording. Watts thought Christians should sing the Psalms the way a Christian would pray them, with Jesus in view. So he rewrote the Psalms in his own verse, and Joy to the world is his version of Psalm 98. Open the King James Bible to that psalm and you can hear the bones of the hymn: "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise." A little further, the sea roars, the floods clap their hands, the hills are joyful together. Why? Because the Lord comes to judge the earth, and the psalm says how: "with righteousness shall he judge the world, and the people with equity." Watts took that and opened his hymn: "Joy to the world! the Lord is come; Let earth receive her King." For Watts the coming king is Jesus, and the hymn looks toward his rule over all the earth. Christians read that coming more than one way. Some hear the first coming, the birth, which is why it found a home at Christmas. Others hear the coming at the end of the age, when the world is set right. Watts himself didn't write it for any one season. And look at the line that becomes ours. Let earth receive her king. Not let the church receive him, not let the good people receive him. The earth. Fields and floods, rocks and hills. The whole created world is invited to make room.
screen: `THE PSALMS, SUNG WITH JESUS IN VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing it any day. Out of season is the point. Say to yourself what today actually is, an ordinary day with no tinsel, and then sing the first line into it, quietly or out loud: joy to the world, the Lord is come. Then sit, and let the psalm's list go by in your mind, one at a time: the sea, the floods, the hills. If you pray, you can make the last line yours: let earth receive her king. If you don't, simply notice the earth under you, holding you up. The bell holds the time.
Joy to the world. Isaac Watts's version of Psalm 98, where the whole earth, seas, floods and hills, rejoices because the Lord comes to judge with righteousness.
Your line: let earth receive her king. Today, step outside once and look at a piece of earth, a tree, a puddle, a patch of sky, as if it were part of the choir. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

900.title: Amazing grace
900.hook: John Newton, a slave-ship captain, later becomes a pastor and joins the abolitionists
900.howItsDone: Amazing Grace is sung across Protestant, Catholic and other churches, at Sunday services, funerals and public gatherings, and Newton is remembered in the Church of England's story of the campaign against the slave trade.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joy to the world, a psalm before it was a carol. Your line was let earth receive her king. Did you look at a piece of earth as part of the choir? Day nine hundred.

The word wretch is a strange one to find in a song people sing at funerals and at weddings. That saved a wretch like me. The man who wrote it did not mean it as a figure of speech. He had been a sailor, a slave trader, and the captain of ships that carried captured Africans across the Atlantic in chains. Later he became a pastor in a small English village. Later still, he stood up in public and said that the trade he had worked in was wicked, and he wanted it ended. Today: Amazing grace.

John Newton's story is often told as a sudden turn: a storm at sea, a terrified prayer, a changed man. That storm did matter to him. But the honest version is slower and harder. After it, Newton kept working in the slave trade, and even captained slave ships, while reading his Bible and keeping a prayer journal. Faith came first. Seeing what he had done came much later. In time he left the sea, was ordained in the Church of England, and served as curate in the village of Olney, where he and the poet William Cowper wrote hymns for their congregation. That's where Amazing grace comes from. Its opening lines: "Amazing grace! (how sweet the sound) That sav'd a wretch like me! I once was lost, but now am found, Was blind, but now I see." Listen for the Gospels in it. Lost and found is the father's cry over the prodigal son in Luke: "he was lost, and is found." Blind but now I see is the man Jesus healed in John, who answers his questioners: "whereas I was blind, now I see." Newton took those two sentences and made them his own. Then he did something harder than writing a hymn. Years after leaving the trade, he published a pamphlet describing what he had seen on the ships, confessing he had taken part, and condemning the trade. He supported William Wilberforce and the campaign to end it. Grace, in Christian teaching, is God's love freely given, never earned. In Newton's life it did not erase the past. It made him able, finally, to look at it.

Here's the practice: confess a wrong you once defended. Not a big public one. Just something you argued for, excused, or laughed along with, that you see differently now. Sit, breathe, and name it plainly to yourself. If you pray, you can bring it to God in your own words, or with Newton's line, I once was lost. If you don't, just let yourself see it clearly, without excuse and without beating yourself up. The bell holds the time.
Amazing grace. John Newton's hymn, written by a former slave-ship captain turned pastor: I once was lost, but now am found, was blind, but now I see.
Your line: I once was lost. Today, if the wrong you named can be put right, take one small step: an apology, a correction, a changed habit. Day nine hundred.

901.title: The Philokalia (1782)
901.hook: two Greek monks gather the Orthodox writings on inner prayer into one collection
901.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians may pray the Jesus Prayer with a prayer rope, a cord of knots, saying the prayer once on each knot, ideally under the guidance of a priest or spiritual father or mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amazing grace, a slave-ship captain's confession. Your line was I once was lost. Did you take a small step to put an old wrong right? Day nine hundred one.

Advice from desert hermits. Notes from abbots on watching your thoughts. Short teachings on how to keep praying while you work, walk and eat. For generations, monks have copied these out by hand, and they sit scattered across monastery libraries, in manuscripts few people could ever see. Then two monks decide it should all be in one place, printed, where anyone who wanted it could find it. They give their anthology a name that sounds less like a manual and more like a love letter. Today's word: Philokalia.

The two monks were Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain, from Mount Athos, and Makarios of Corinth, a bishop. Their book gathers writings by Orthodox teachers across the centuries on what the Orthodox call watchfulness: guarding the heart, noticing thoughts as they arrive, and praying inwardly. The title is Greek, and it carries our line: Philokalia, love of the beautiful, or love of the good. The beautiful here is not a painting. It is God, and a heart made quiet enough to love God. At the center of much of the book is a very short prayer, the Jesus Prayer. Orthodox Christians pray it in words like these: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. It grows out of the Gospels. In Luke, a blind man by the road near Jericho calls out, "Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me." And in Jesus's parable the tax collector stands far off in the temple and prays only, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Paul tells the Thessalonians: "Pray without ceasing." The writers of the Philokalia take that seriously. How do you pray without ceasing? You give the mind one short prayer, said slowly, often with the breath, until it is less something you say and more something the heart keeps saying. The writers are honest that this is not a technique for calm. They warn against chasing experiences, and they say a beginner needs a guide. Catholics have their own long tradition of contemplative prayer, and some Protestants pray short breath prayers too. But this collection comes from the Orthodox, and the way of prayer it teaches is theirs.

Here's the practice: the Jesus Prayer, for the length of the sit, and longer later if you like. Sit still and let your breathing slow. If you pray, you can say it silently: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, on the in-breath, have mercy on me, on the out-breath. When your mind wanders, come back without fuss. If you don't pray, simply breathe, and on each out-breath let the word mercy pass through. The bell holds the time.
Philokalia. A Greek word meaning love of the beautiful, and the name of an Orthodox anthology on inner prayer and watchfulness of the heart.

Your line: love of the beautiful. Today, while waiting for something, a kettle, a light, a page to load, use the moment for one slow breath and one short line instead of a scroll. Day nine hundred one.

902.title: Paisius Velichkovsky
902.hook: a Ukrainian monk translates the Philokalia into Slavonic and renews Russian monasteries
902.howItsDone: In Orthodox Christianity, people may have a spiritual father or mother, often a priest or monastic, to whom they bring their thoughts and confession, and some travel to monasteries to ask an elder for guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Philokalia, the Orthodox anthology on inner prayer. Your line was love of the beautiful. Did you trade one scroll for one slow breath? Day nine hundred two.

On Mount Athos, the Holy Mountain in Greece, a monk from Ukraine sits with two texts side by side. One is an old Slavonic translation of a Greek writer on prayer, the same kind of writing we met yesterday. The other is the Greek itself. They don't match. Copyists have muddled the Slavonic until some sentences barely make sense. He had walked out of a theological academy in Kyiv without finishing, not failing, just restless: the lectures were full of argument, and he wanted to learn how to pray. Now the books his own people pray from turn out to be blurred. So he sets out to learn Greek properly and fix them. Today: Paisius Velichkovsky.

Paisius had looked for a living teacher of prayer and, by his own account, mostly failed to find one. So he learned Greek well enough to read the old writers on prayer for himself. Other monks began gathering around him, first on Athos and later in monasteries in Moldavia, in what is now Romania. He ran those communities in two languages, with services and readings so that Slavic and Romanian monks could both follow. And he gave his life to translation. Working from Greek manuscripts, he rendered the teachings of the Philokalia into Church Slavonic, the language of worship in the Russian and other Slavic churches. Now a Russian monk who had never seen Athos could read the desert fathers on watchfulness and the Jesus Prayer. Paisius never went to Russia to lead it himself. His disciples did. They carried his books and his way of life north, and with them came our line: the startsy. A starets, in Russian, is an elder, a monk whose long practice of prayer lets him guide others. You go to him, you open your heart, you tell him your thoughts, and he gives a word for you. It isn't a lecture. It's a relationship, closer to a doctor and a patient, or a parent and a child. Paisius taught that this kind of obedience to a wise guide protects a beginner on the road into inner prayer, because a beginner left alone easily fools himself. Through his disciples, elders became a living presence in Russian monasteries, and ordinary people, peasants and nobles, began making journeys to ask them for a word. The restless student who couldn't find a teacher ended up helping to form the teachers who came after him.

Here's the practice: learn from an elder. Sit, and bring to mind someone older or wiser who has helped you, a grandparent, a teacher, a pastor, a friend who has been through things. Hear their voice. Remember one thing they said that stayed. If you pray, you can give thanks for them, or pray for them by name. If you don't, just hold them with gratitude, and think of one question you'd still like to ask. The bell holds the time.
Paisius Velichkovsky. A Ukrainian monk who translated the Philokalia into Church Slavonic and whose disciples carried the tradition of elders into Russian monasteries.
Your line: the startsy. Today, ask that question. Call, text or visit someone older and wiser, and ask them for a word about something real in your life. Then listen. Day nine hundred two.

903.title: Tikhon of Zadonsk
903.hook: a bishop who gave away his bishop's comforts to live simply among the poor
903.howItsDone: The Orthodox Church remembers Tikhon of Zadonsk as a saint with feast days in its calendar, and his writings on prayer and on seeing God in ordinary things are still read in Orthodox homes and monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paisius Velichkovsky and the elders. Your line was the startsy. Did you ask someone older and wiser for a word? Day nine hundred three.

There's a story told about a Russian bishop and a quarrel. A proud nobleman, losing an argument with him, struck him across the face. The bishop did not strike back, and did not storm out. Tradition says he bowed down to the floor in front of the man and asked his forgiveness for having provoked him. The nobleman, shaken, ended up on his knees too. The bishop was a man who had already stepped away from what a bishop gets: the palace, the standing, the comforts. Today: Tikhon of Zadonsk.
screen: `A BISHOP WHO GAVE IT ALL UP.`

segments.voice: Tikhon was a Russian Orthodox bishop who served the diocese of Voronezh. He worked hard at it, opening schools and teaching his clergy, until his health broke down. Then he asked to step aside, and went to live in a monastery at Zadonsk, near the river Don. There he lived very simply, in a plain cell, and gave away what came to him, food, clothes, money, to the poor who lined up at his door. He visited prisoners. He sat with peasants. People came to him for counsel, as they would to one of the elders we met yesterday. His writings return again and again to one habit of mind. Everything around you, he taught, can point to God, even the plainest things you pass every day. He wrote a book on just that, gathering spiritual lessons from ordinary things. And it leads to our line: all is from God. Tikhon did not mean that every cruelty is God's wish. He meant that nothing, not even trouble, falls outside God's care, so that a person can receive both good days and bad ones with trust. It echoes Paul's letter to the Romans: "all things work together for good to them that love God." It also sheds light on the bow after the slap. If even an insult can be received from God's hand, then, as Tikhon saw it, there was no need to defend his dignity with his fists. The Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky admired him, and some readers see Tikhon behind the gentle elder Zosima in The Brothers Karamazov. The Orthodox Church honors him as a saint.

Here's the practice: give up one comfort. Choose something small you'd normally reach for today, the cushion, the snack, the extra blanket, the second coffee, and let it go. Sit without it now, and notice what you feel. If you pray, you can offer the small lack to God, or think of someone who goes without every day. If you don't, simply notice the gap, and think of who might use what you didn't. The bell holds the time.
Tikhon of Zadonsk. A Russian bishop who stepped aside, lived simply in a monastery, gave to the poor, and taught that everything can point to God.

Your line: all is from God. That ends a week of preachers, poets and monks: Whitefield in the fields, Edwards and the heart, Joy to the world, Amazing grace, the Philokalia, Paisius, and Tikhon. Today, pick one ordinary object and ask what it might teach. Day nine hundred three.

myth: Tikhon taught that every cruelty is God's wish
he meant that nothing, not even trouble, falls outside God's care.
Tikhon wrote about finding spiritual lessons in ordinary things
ordinary things in the world could all point to God.
Tikhon lived in a bishop's palace to the end of his life
he stepped aside and lived in a plain cell at Zadonsk, giving away what came to him.
trapdoor: what you thought: a Russian saint with an unfamiliar name.
what it means: a bishop who stepped aside to live simply among the poor, teaching that all is from God.
what a scholar hears: a writer on seeing God in everyday things, admired by Dostoevsky, whom some readers see behind the elder Zosima.
